turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Mr. Ellison. You're 66, and they booked you for a check-up. How've you been?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty good, I guess. I don't know, doctor. June's the one who called.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm June, I live with him and help with meals and the pills. He's been funny on the stairs.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Funny how?
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He stops on the landing and presses his chest. Most mornings. Well, actually, not every morning, but a lot, since it got cold.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not having chest pain. She makes it sound worse. Those stairs are steep, that's all.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. You wouldn't call it pain. When you stop and put your hand there, what do you feel?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe nothing. Can't we just check the pressure?
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He told me it was tight. Last week, walking fast to catch the bus, he had to stand still a minute.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah. If I walk fast, or I climb, there's a tight feeling across my chest. Not pain. It lets up when I stop.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me play that back. Tightness across the chest with fast walking or stairs, it eases if you rest, and you don't experience it as pain. Did I hear that right?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's right.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the tightness been happening?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. The tomatoes in the yard were ridiculous this year, I've been watering every evening. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Glad the tomatoes worked out. About the chest, though — days, weeks, months?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know. A few weeks, maybe? I'm terrible with dates.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's two months. Easy. Started when the mornings turned cold.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): You don't agree, and there's no firm start date. I'll record it as roughly a few weeks to two months.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure. I guess.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does that tight feeling ever come on when you're sitting still?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): My left knee's been aching bad. That's half of why I take the stairs slow. Acts up when it's damp.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the knee for now. The tightness — on the couch, does it happen, or only when you're moving?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Only when I'm moving. Fast walking, stairs. I stop and it's gone in a minute, maybe two. Not sitting.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sweating with it, or nausea?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't think so.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does get short of breath. You'll see him at the rail, breathing through his mouth.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not short of breath. I just don't rush. I don't know why she keeps saying that.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): So she reports shortness of breath and you deny it. I'll leave that as disagreed. Do you have a cough?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about medicines. What are you actually taking?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): A blood pressure tablet. And aspirin, but it's on and off. I forget.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Blood pressure one is lisinopril. I set it next to his coffee every morning.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse read me your list just now. She has lisinopril twenty milligrams, once a day. That what's on the bottle?
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No. That's not right. Our bottle says ten milligrams. I've been giving him the ten every morning for a long time.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. It's a little white pill. I don't look at the milligrams.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the nurse's list says twenty and June says the bottle is ten. I won't choose until I see the bottle. Are you swallowing one every morning?
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Every morning, with breakfast. Yes.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. If I'm rushing out I might skip it. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the aspirin — what strength, and how often do you really take it?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): The baby aspirin, 81. Some weeks I take it every day, some weeks I skip three or four days. On and off.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I've been after him to take it daily. He puts it in his pocket. He misses half the days, at least.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Aspirin 81 milligrams by mouth, then, but neither of you can say how many days he actually gets it. Any other medicine? Cholesterol pill, water pill?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just those two.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the lisinopril is for high blood pressure you've had a while?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Years. I couldn't tell you how many. They picked it up at a check-up.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any diabetes that you know of?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Not that anyone's told me.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to listen to your heart and lungs, and I'll take the pressure myself.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): With me it's 146 over 88. Pulse is 72 and regular. Oxygen saturation is 97 percent.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heart rhythm is regular and I don't hear a murmur. Lungs are clear both sides. No tenderness when I press on the chest wall.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): So that's good? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): The exam itself is reassuring. The story is the part that concerns me. Tightness when you exert yourself, gone when you stop — my working impression is this could be angina. Not a final label.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Angina means his heart, right?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can be a heart-related tightness. I can't confirm that today. I'd like an ECG before you go, plus bloods, a metabolic panel and a cholesterol panel.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Blood today? I already had coffee. Is that gonna mess it up?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee's fine, no need to fast. We'll get the blood drawn and the ECG done before you leave.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Should he stop the aspirin until you know?
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it. Keep taking the aspirin, and try not to skip, and keep taking the lisinopril. Bring that bottle to the desk so we can correct the dose on the chart.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): When the tight feeling starts I just stop walking. That's been working.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep doing that, don't push through it. If it starts while you're resting, or it hangs on more than a few minutes, or you get sweaty or sick with it, call 911.
[SEG0061] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll stay with him on the stairs at home.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): I want to see you back in one week to go over the ECG and the labs.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): A week? What if it gets worse before that?
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it gets worse before that, come back sooner, and if it's happening at rest go to the ER. Otherwise I'll see you in one week.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I don't know, doctor. I hope you're wrong about the heart thing.
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): I might be. The tests will help. June, that bottle really does matter.
[SEG0067] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll stick it in my purse tonight so it actually gets here.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. Appreciate you seeing me.

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

bad.reason: Lisinopril for high blood pressure is supported, but frequency 'every morning' is disputed by patient skipping some days.
bad.text: lisinopril (route=oral, frequency=every morning, indication=high blood pressure, status=currently_used, reported_by=caregiver)

omissions.text: Lisinopril dose is not established: nurse list said 20 mg once daily, but caregiver reports the home bottle says 10 mg and the doctor deferred choosing a dose until seeing the bottle.
Heart rate was noted to be regular ('Pulse is 72 and regular'). The regularity of the pulse is not captured in the vital signs.
The doctor instructed that if symptoms occur at rest, the patient should go to the ER; this ER instruction is not separately captured, only the earlier 911 advice and 'come back sooner.'
The planned follow-up was specifically to review the ECG and lab results in one week.

omissions.text: Lisinopril dose is not established: nurse list said 20 mg once daily, but caregiver says the home bottle says 10 mg and she has been giving 10 mg every morning for a long time; doctor would not choose a dose until seeing the bottle. The recorded medication entry omits the dose discrepancy and unresolved current dose.

Patient reports lisinopril is not taken every day: he takes it 'most days' and may skip it if rushing out. The recorded medication frequency as every morning is therefore inaccurate without noting missed doses.

Aspirin adherence detail missing/wrong: patient said some weeks he takes aspirin 81 mg every day and some weeks skips 3 or 4 days; caregiver said he misses at least half the days. Recording only 'on and off' misses the extent of nonadherence.
Patient denied shortness of breath, while caregiver reported it; this explicit denial is not separately recorded as a negative finding, only as a disputed positive symptom.
Doctor documented exam as reassuring; this reassuring interpretation of the physical exam is not recorded.
Doctor said bloods and ECG would be done before the patient leaves, and coffee was fine/no need to fast for the tests. These immediate timing/pre-test instructions are not recorded.

Return precautions were broader than recorded: if symptoms get worse before the scheduled week follow-up, come back sooner, and if happening at rest go to the ER. The 'come back sooner if worse' detail is not fully captured.
